analysis.one_liner: Requires automakers to raise new-car and light-truck fuel mileage 20 to 40 percent above their 1988 levels.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from September 1990 until the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every automaker to raise the average fuel economy of its new passenger cars by 20 percent over its 1988 fleet by model year 1995, and by 40 percent by model year 2001, with floors and ceilings of 27.5–40 mpg and 33–45 mpg respectively [S3]. It applied the same percentage improvement approach to light trucks, whose fuel economy had stagnated, and removed the scheduled end of light-truck fuel economy rules after model year 1995 [S3]. It also doubled civil penalties for automakers that repeatedly violated the standards, directed the EPA to compare lab fuel-economy tests with real-world driving, and ordered studies on how to regulate fuel economy beyond 2001 [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save on gasoline over the life of their vehicles — the bill's findings cite earlier efficiency gains saving drivers close to $30 billion, and project a 20-to-40-percent improvement would save 49.1 billion gallons of fuel between 1995 and 2001 [S3]. The country would also cut oil imports and carbon dioxide emissions, which the bill's findings project at 483.5 million tons over that period [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every manufacturer would have to improve its fleet's average fuel economy by 20 percent over its own 1988 level for model years 1995–2000 (cars: no less than 27.5 mpg, no more than 40), and 40 percent for 2001 and later (no less than 33, no more than 45 mpg), with a 30-percent floor on any later downward adjustment [S3].

Light trucks — about one-third of new passenger vehicle sales by 1990 — would be subject to the same percentage-improvement approach, reaching 20–30 mpg for 1995–2000 and 24–35 mpg for 2001 and thereafter, ending years in which they escaped strict legislated standards [S3].
Civil penalties for violating the fuel economy standard would be doubled for a manufacturer that fell short by half a mile per gallon or more in three consecutive model years [S3].

The EPA would have to report annually on how far official fuel-economy test numbers diverge from what real drivers actually get, and how much fuel economy deteriorates over a vehicle's life [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of engineering more efficient fleets, and oil companies would face lower gasoline demand — the bill projects 49.1 billion gallons of fuel savings between 1995 and 2001 [S3]. Consumers would likely pay somewhat higher vehicle prices upfront, though the bill directs the Transportation Secretary to weigh those costs against operating-cost savings in any later adjustments [S3].

drawbacks.text: Higher fuel economy generally raises the upfront price of a vehicle, and the bill requires the Transportation Secretary to weigh 'the economic impact of the standard on the manufacturers and on the consumers' and any loss of vehicle utility or competition before modifying the 2001-and-later standards — an acknowledgment that the costs are real and fall partly on buyers [S3].

The percentage-based design ties each manufacturer's target to its own 1988 baseline, so a company that had already made efficient cars in 1988 would have to improve from a higher starting point, while the ceilings of 40 and 45 mpg would cap how much the most efficient makers had to do [S3].

The standards for 2001 and later could be raised or lowered through a rulemaking after fiscal 1995, which — even with the 30-percent floor — left long-term targets subject to later political decisions [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains to drivers and the public were large and quantified in the bill itself — tens of billions of dollars in fuel savings and hundreds of millions of tons of avoided carbon dioxide — while the costs, chiefly higher sticker prices and compliance spending by automakers, would have been partly offset by fuel savings over each vehicle's life. The bill's main design weakness was tying targets to each manufacturer's own 1988 baseline and leaving post-2001 standards open to later rulemaking. On balance, the benefits to ordinary drivers clearly outweighed the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee, and it died there — no hearing-driven markup, no floor vote — when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on September 10, 1990, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
Four days later, on September 14, 1990, it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].
The bill had 44 cosponsors, 40 of 257 House Democrats and 4 of 175 House Republicans [S4].
Boxer introduced the bill with 14 original cosponsors, including Nancy Pelosi, Edward Markey, Chuck Schumer, Pete Stark, and Leon Panetta [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers avoided mandatory fleet-wide fuel economy improvements and doubled penalties for repeat violations, and oil companies avoided reduced gasoline demand. Drivers continued to bear the fuel costs the bill's findings projected would have been saved.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 original cosponsors, including Pelosi, Markey, and Schumer

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (with jurisdiction over fuel economy standards)
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and it died in committee

against.name: U.S. automakers
against.what_they_did: Opposed stricter corporate average fuel economy standards and pressed Congress against raising them

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 40 of the 44 cosponsors were Democrats, with only 4 Republicans — and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat aligned with the auto industry, with no vote ever recorded to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would have required every manufacturer to lift its fleet's average fuel economy 20 percent over its 1988 level by 1995 and 40 percent by 2001, and doubled penalties for repeat violators. Compliance would have required engineering spending, but the bill's own findings show the cost lands partly on buyers as higher prices while fuel savings flow back to them.

The bill's findings project that a 20-to-40-percent efficiency improvement would save 49.1 billion gallons of gasoline between 1995 and 2001, cutting directly into fuel sales. The industry benefits when vehicles burn more gasoline, so its interest ran against drivers' savings at the pump.

The bill would have required the Energy Department to give every dealer at least 100 consumer fuel-economy booklets a year, a small compliance burden, but more efficient cars could have been easier or harder to sell depending on gas prices.
